intro:
The best laptop power bank for most people is the Anker 737 (PowerCore 24K): Anker rates its single USB-C port at up to 140 watts and its capacity at 24,000 mAh, about 86 Wh, which is under the 100 Wh airline limit. That is enough output for nearly any USB-C laptop and about one full charge of a 14-inch machine.

A laptop power bank is not a phone bank with a bigger number on the box. Two figures decide everything: the wattage of its best USB-C port, which sets whether your laptop charges at all, and its watt-hours, which set for how long. This guide ranks six packs, then explains wattage matching, mAh-to-Wh math, airline rules, cables and when a small power station is the better buy.
quickAnswer: Buy the Anker 737 for one laptop at full speed, the Anker Prime 26K 300W for two laptops at once, the Anker 25K 165W if you hate carrying cables, the UGREEN Nexode 200W for value, and the Baseus Blade 100W for a slim ultrabook bank. Match the bank's per-port USB-C wattage to your laptop charger and expect about one full laptop charge.

Power banks get renamed often, so confirm capacity, per-port wattage and total output on the listing.

For a whole household's phones during a blackout, see our [portable chargers for power outages](/best-portable-chargers-for-power-outages/) instead; laptop banks are heavier than you need for phones.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Laptop Power Banks in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
### Best Overall: Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K)

The Anker 737 gets the two important numbers right. Anker rates it at 24,000 mAh, around 86 Wh, which is roughly one full charge for a 14-inch laptop, and its USB-C port supports up to 140 watts under USB PD 3.1. That is enough to charge even a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed with a 240-watt cable.

It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, but 140 watts is the total, so plugging in a phone next to a big laptop splits the output. The built-in display shows remaining charge plus live watts in and out, which tells you at a glance whether a cable is throttling the laptop. It refills quickly from a high-watt USB-C wall charger. The downside is weight: it is a dense brick you will feel in a bag.

**Pros:** 140W from one USB-C port; full speed for a 16-inch MacBook Pro; live wattage display; under 100 Wh; fast USB-C recharge.

**Cons:** heavy for its size; 140W is shared across ports; full speed needs a PD 3.1 laptop and cable.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Anker+737+Power+Bank+PowerCore+24K&tag=sktiger-20)

### Most Powerful: Anker Prime Power Bank 26K 300W

The Anker Prime 26K is for people who outgrow a single 140-watt port. Anker rates it at 26,250 mAh, just under the 100 Wh airline ceiling, with up to 300 watts total across its ports and up to 140 watts on any single USB-C port.

In practice it can feed two large laptops at high speed at once, or a laptop, tablet and phone without the usual slowdown when a new device is plugged in. A display shows what each port is doing. For one laptop and a phone it is overkill and heavier than the 737. For couples traveling with two work machines, photographers charging a laptop and a camera charger, or anyone running two screens away from an outlet, it is the most capable bank you can carry on a plane.

**Pros:** 300W total; two laptops at high wattage; under 100 Wh; per-port display.

**Cons:** top-of-market pricing; heavier than single-laptop banks; more than one laptop needs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Anker+Prime+Power+Bank+26K+300W&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Travel: Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K 165W

The most common reason a bank fails to charge a laptop is the cable, not the bank. Anker's 25K 165W solves that by building USB-C cables into the body, one of them retractable, so the bank always carries its own 100-watt-class connection. Anker rates it at 25,000 mAh, around 90 Wh, with up to 165 watts total and extra USB-C and USB-A ports.

A single laptop gets up to roughly 100 watts, which suits nearly every 13- and 14-inch machine and most 16-inch Windows laptops; a 16-inch MacBook Pro will charge slower than its 140-watt brick allows. A display shows remaining charge. If a built-in cable gets damaged you cannot swap it, but the standard ports give you a fallback.

**Pros:** built-in USB-C cables; 165W total; about 90 Wh; extra ports.

**Cons:** about 100W to one laptop; fixed cables; bulkier than slim banks.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Anker+Laptop+Power+Bank+25K+165W+built-in+cable&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value Multi-Device: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25000mAh 200W

UGREEN built its name on Nexode USB-C chargers, and this 25,000 mAh bank applies the same approach. UGREEN rates it at up to 200 watts total, so it can charge a laptop at high speed while still feeding a phone or tablet without the sharp slowdown smaller banks show. At about 90 Wh it sits comfortably under the airline limit, and a display shows remaining charge.

The 200-watt figure is the total; a single port delivers less, so compare the per-port rating on the listing with your laptop charger. For most 13- to 15-inch laptops that is not an issue. UGREEN sells several similarly named Nexode banks with different outputs, so confirm the 200W model. It usually costs a little less than Anker for similar output.

**Pros:** 200W total; laptop plus phone at once; about 90 Wh; usually priced below comparable Anker models.

**Cons:** lower per-port maximum; heavier than single-laptop banks; easy to buy the wrong Nexode.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=UGREEN+Nexode+Power+Bank+25000mAh+200W&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Slim Bank: Baseus Blade 100W 20000mAh

Most laptop banks are thick bricks. The Baseus Blade is a flat slab closer in profile to a small tablet, built to slide into a laptop sleeve or thin briefcase. Baseus rates it at 20,000 mAh, about 72 Wh, with up to 100 watts of USB-C PD output, enough for most 13- and 14-inch laptops at or near full speed and roughly one full charge of a 50 Wh ultrabook.

It has a display and multiple USB-C and USB-A ports. The trade-offs come with the shape: less capacity than the 25,000 mAh banks, a wide footprint, and 100 watts is not enough to run a 16-inch performance laptop at full speed.

**Pros:** thin enough for a sleeve; 100W USB-C; charge display; several ports.

**Cons:** smallest capacity here; not enough for 140W laptops at full speed; wide footprint.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Baseus+Blade+100W+laptop+power+bank+20000mAh&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Remote Work and Outages: Anker SOLIX C300 DC

The SOLIX C300 DC sits between a power bank and a power station, and it is the most efficient way past the 100 Wh airline ceiling for laptop users. Anker rates its LFP battery at 288 Wh, roughly three times the largest legal bank, and it charges laptops directly through high-watt USB-C ports instead of through an inverter and your wall charger.

Skipping that DC-to-AC-to-DC round trip means more stored energy reaches the laptop, so three to four full laptop charges plus phones is a reasonable planning figure. There are no AC outlets, which rules out monitors or anything with a wall plug, it cannot fly, and it is far heavier than a bank. For a cabin, a van or a multi-day outage, it is the right size.

**Pros:** 288 Wh; high-watt USB-C ports; LFP cells rated for long cycle life; no inverter losses for USB devices.

**Cons:** cannot fly; no AC outlets; much heavier than a bank.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Anker+SOLIX+C300+DC+power+bank+station&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Power Bank Do You Need for a Laptop?
sections.body:
Start with the charger that came with your laptop. Its wattage is the most the laptop will ever ask for, and it is the best guide to the bank you need.

### Typical laptop charger wattage

| Laptop type | Typical charger |
| --- | --- |
| MacBook Air, 13-inch ultrabooks | 30 to 65W |
| 14-inch performance laptops | 65 to 100W |
| 16-inch MacBook Pro | 140W |
| Gaming laptops | 180 to 330W barrel chargers |

### How USB-C PD sets the wattage

Laptop banks talk to laptops through USB Power Delivery. The two negotiate a voltage and current, and that sets the watts. Classic PD tops out at 100 watts (20 volts at 5 amps). PD 3.1 Extended Power Range adds 28, 36 and 48 volt levels, which is how a port reaches 140 watts or more, but only when the laptop and cable both support it. Otherwise it falls back to 100 watts or less.

### Per-port output beats total output

A bank sold as 200 or 300 watts usually quotes all ports combined. The most one port can deliver is often 100 or 140 watts. A 300-watt bank will not charge one laptop at 300 watts; it charges several devices at once without throttling. Read the per-port figure first.

### How close do you need to match?

A bank below your charger's rating still charges, just slower, and under heavy load the laptop may hold steady instead of gaining. Some laptops show a slow-charger warning, and a few refuse below a certain wattage. Aim for a single-port output of at least two-thirds of your charger's rating, and match it fully if you work hard unplugged.

sections.heading: How Many Wh Does a Laptop Power Bank Need?
sections.body:
Most people need 70 to 100 Wh, which delivers about one full charge of a typical laptop. To convert a bank's mAh rating, multiply by the cell voltage (usually 3.6 or 3.7 volts) and divide by 1,000. A 24,000 mAh bank is about 86 to 89 Wh; a 20,000 mAh bank about 72 to 74 Wh.

### You do not get every watt-hour

A laptop bank has to boost its cells from about 3.6 volts to 20 volts or more, and that loses energy as heat. A realistic planning figure is 70 to 85 percent delivered for a good bank, at the lower end when charging at high wattage. Cheap banks with inflated ratings can do much worse.

| Rated capacity | Approx. Wh (3.6 V) | Delivered (70 to 85%) | Typical result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20,000 mAh | ~72 Wh | ~50 to 61 Wh | About one ultrabook charge |
| 24,000 mAh | ~86 Wh | ~60 to 73 Wh | About one 14-inch laptop charge |
| 25,000 mAh | ~90 Wh | ~63 to 77 Wh | One charge plus a phone |
| 26,250 mAh | ~95 Wh | ~66 to 80 Wh | Near the airline ceiling |
| 288 Wh station | 288 Wh | ~230 to 245 Wh | Three to four laptop charges |

### Compare with your laptop battery

A 13-inch MacBook Air sits in the low 50s of watt-hours, a 14-inch MacBook Pro around 70 Wh, and a 16-inch MacBook Pro right at the 100 Wh legal maximum for a laptop battery. Windows ultrabooks usually fall between 50 and 75 Wh. So an airline-legal bank roughly doubles a modern laptop's unplugged day; it will not triple it.

### Sizing for a set number of hours

For a target like one hour of backup, use the laptop's real draw, not its charger rating. A light-use ultrabook might average 10 to 20 watts, so even a 72 Wh bank covers several hours. A performance laptop under load can pull 60 watts or more, and a 140-watt machine at full tilt can drain a bank in about an hour. Divide the bank's delivered Wh by your average watts to estimate hours.

sections.heading: Can You Take a Laptop Power Bank on a Plane?
sections.body:
Yes, in carry-on only. Under FAA and IATA guidance, spare lithium batteries, which includes every power bank, must stay out of checked bags.

| Battery size | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Up to 100 Wh | Carry-on, no airline approval needed |
| 100 to 160 Wh | Airline approval required, two spares max |
| Over 160 Wh | Not allowed as a passenger item |
| Any size | Never in checked luggage |

### Make sure the Wh figure is printed

Screeners check the watt-hour rating on the case. If only mAh is shown, they may do the math or refuse the bank. Reputable brands print the figure, and every bank here is designed to fall under 100 Wh. Be wary of banks whose ratings look too large for their size.

### In-flight use is tightening

After a series of cabin battery fires, a growing number of airlines restrict charging from power banks during flight, require banks to stay visible rather than in an overhead bin, or ban in-flight use outright. Policies vary and change often, so check your carrier before counting on charging at cruising altitude. Charging at the gate is almost always fine.

### Why 100 Wh is the practical ceiling

Roughly 26,000 to 27,000 mAh is the most a bank can hold and still fly freely. Anything bigger is a power station, which is why the jump to one, such as the SOLIX C300 DC or the stations in our [portable power station guide](/best-portable-power-station/), is a big step rather than a slightly larger bank.

sections.heading: Which Power Banks Work With Windows Laptops and MacBooks?
sections.body:
Any bank with enough USB-C PD wattage works with any laptop that charges over USB-C, whether it runs Windows 11, ChromeOS or macOS. The operating system does not matter; the charging port does.

### Windows laptops

Many current Windows ultrabooks charge over USB-C at 45 to 100 watts, and a 100-watt bank like the Baseus Blade or the Anker 25K 165W covers them. Budget models, older laptops and some business machines still use a round barrel plug, which a USB-C bank cannot feed directly. Popular lines like the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim have shipped with both styles depending on the model and year, so check your own charger: a USB-C plug marked with 65 watts means a 65-watt-or-better bank will work.

### Gaming laptops

Gaming laptops, such as models with RTX-class graphics, usually ship with high-watt barrel or slim-tip chargers well above what any USB-C bank delivers. Some also accept USB-C charging but cap it near 100 watts, which keeps the battery topped during light work but cannot sustain gaming loads.

### MacBooks with MagSafe

MacBooks that charge through MagSafe also charge through their USB-C or Thunderbolt ports, so a USB-C bank works without a MagSafe connection. A 14-inch MacBook Pro charges well from a 100-watt bank; a 16-inch model needs a 140-watt port and a 240-watt cable for full speed, which points to the Anker 737 or Prime.

### Is there anything faster than 140 watts per port?

Not meaningfully for laptops today. 140 watts is what USB-C laptops commonly request at the top end, so a bank's advantage beyond that comes from total output across ports, not a faster single port.

sections.heading: Do You Need a Special Cable for a Laptop Power Bank?
sections.body:
Yes, often. A high-watt bank is only as fast as the cable plugged into it.

### Cable ratings

Ordinary USB-C cables carry 3 amps, which caps them at 60 watts. Passing more needs an e-marker chip that tells the bank the cable handles 5 amps, unlocking 100 watts at 20 volts. Reaching 140 watts under PD 3.1 takes a cable rated for 240 watts. Many cables bundled with phones are 60-watt cables that quietly throttle a laptop bank.

### Diagnosing slow charging

If the laptop charges slowly, suspect the cable first. Buy one explicitly rated for 100 watts, or 240 watts for a 140-watt laptop, from a reputable brand, and keep it with the bank. Short cables are slightly more efficient. A cheap inline USB-C power meter shows exactly what the bank and laptop negotiated, and banks with displays, like the Anker 737, show it on the bank.

### When the laptop draws more than the bank supplies

Under heavy load, a laptop can draw more than the bank provides and slowly drain even while plugged in. That is not a fault; the bank still extends runtime a lot. For hours of full-power work like video rendering on a 16-inch machine, a station with an AC outlet and your original charger is the better tool.

sections.heading: Can a Laptop Power Bank Charge Several Devices and Recharge Fast?
sections.body:
Yes, if it has enough total output and fast input.

### Charging a laptop, phone and tablet together

A 140-watt bank sending 100 watts to a laptop has only 40 watts left for everything else, and plugging in a second device makes many banks renegotiate every port, briefly cutting power. Banks with 200 to 300 watts of total output, like the UGREEN Nexode and Anker Prime, are built for this. More ports do not add capacity, though: three devices drain a 90 Wh bank three times faster. On a long flight, charge the laptop first.

### Pass-through charging

Pass-through lets the bank charge your devices while it is plugged in itself. At a hotel with one outlet, the wall feeds the bank and the bank feeds the laptop. It adds heat and cell wear, so do not use it as a permanent desk setup. Implementations vary, so check the listing.

### Recharge speed

An 86 Wh bank that refills at 20 watts takes most of a day; one that accepts 100 watts or more over USB-C refills in around an hour. High-output banks need a matching wall charger to reach that speed. Fast input also helps during outages, when power returns in short windows, and with solar: our [solar power bank guide](/best-solar-power-bank/) covers when panel charging is worth it.

sections.heading: When Is a Power Station Better Than a Laptop Power Bank?
sections.body:
A power bank is the right tool for travel, a single long day and most people's outage plans. It stops being right when you need several laptop charges in a row, need an AC outlet, or work remotely for days. Then the 100 Wh ceiling is the limit, and the next step is a 250 to 300 Wh station holding about three times the energy.

### DC-only stations

The Anker SOLIX C300 DC charges laptops directly over high-watt USB-C, which is more efficient than plugging your laptop charger into an AC outlet. For a cabin, a van or a home office during a long outage, that means three or four laptop charges plus phones and a router.

### When you need AC

To run a monitor, a modem with a wall brick or a CPAP, choose a station with outlets. Our [battery pack with AC outlet guide](/best-battery-pack-with-ac-outlet/) covers small packs, our [Anker SOLIX power station guide](/best-anker-solix-power-station/) covers bigger sizes, and for a desk setup a [UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) switches over instantly when the grid drops. CPAP users should size with our [CPAP battery backup guide](/best-battery-backup-for-cpap/).

### The trade-off

A station weighs several times as much as a bank, cannot fly and is overkill for a flight or a conference day.

mistakes.title: Buying on Total Wattage Instead of Per-Port Output
mistakes.body: A 200- or 300-watt bank usually quotes all ports combined, while the one USB-C port your laptop uses may top out at 100 or 140 watts. Match the per-port figure to your laptop charger, and treat the total as how many devices the bank can feed at once.

mistakes.title: Using a 60-Watt Cable
mistakes.body: Ordinary USB-C cables carry 3 amps, capping them at 60 watts no matter what the bank can do. Laptops above 60 watts need a 5-amp e-marked cable rated for 100 watts, and 140-watt laptops need a 240-watt cable. The wrong cable is the top cause of slow laptop charging.

mistakes.title: Expecting Several Laptop Charges From One Bank
mistakes.body: Airline-legal banks hold at most 100 Wh, and conversion losses mean a laptop sees roughly 70 to 85 percent of that. Plan on about one full charge for a typical laptop. If you need three or four, a small power station is the honest answer.

mistakes.title: Packing a Power Bank in Checked Luggage
mistakes.body: Spare lithium batteries, including every power bank, must travel in carry-on bags under FAA and IATA rules, and banks found in checked bags are usually removed. Keep the bank with you, make sure its Wh rating is printed on the case, and check your airline's in-flight policy.

mistakes.title: Assuming Every Laptop Charges Over USB-C
mistakes.body: Many budget and gaming laptops use barrel connectors and cannot charge from a USB-C bank, and some USB-C models cap charging near 100 watts. Check your laptop for USB-C Power Delivery support and its maximum wattage before buying, or the bank may only charge your phone.

faqs.q: What is the best laptop power bank?
faqs.a: The Anker 737 (PowerCore 24K) is the best laptop power bank for most people. Its USB-C port supports up to 140 watts, enough for nearly any USB-C laptop at full speed, and its roughly 86 Wh capacity flies without airline approval. Choose the Anker Prime 26K for two laptops or the Baseus Blade for a slim bank.

faqs.q: What power bank do you need for a laptop?
faqs.a: You need a USB-C PD power bank whose single-port output is at least two-thirds of your laptop charger's wattage, ideally a full match, with 70 to 100 Wh of capacity. Ultrabooks usually need 30 to 65 watts, 14-inch performance laptops 65 to 100 watts, and a 16-inch MacBook Pro 140 watts.

faqs.q: How many Wh power bank do I need for a laptop?
faqs.a: Most laptops are well served by a 70 to 100 Wh power bank, which delivers about one full charge after conversion losses of 15 to 30 percent. Laptop batteries typically hold 50 to 75 Wh, and a 16-inch MacBook Pro about 100 Wh. For three or more charges, you need a 250 Wh-plus power station.

faqs.q: Can a power bank run a laptop?
faqs.a: Yes, a power bank can run a laptop that charges over USB-C, as long as its per-port wattage covers the laptop's workload. Under light use, a 65-watt bank keeps most ultrabooks running and charging. Under heavy loads like gaming, the laptop may draw more than the bank supplies and slowly drain, though runtime still improves a lot.

faqs.q: Can I take a laptop power bank on a plane?
faqs.a: Yes, in carry-on luggage only. Under FAA and IATA rules, banks up to 100 Wh need no approval, banks from 100 to 160 Wh need airline approval and are limited to two, and anything over 160 Wh is banned. Power banks are never allowed in checked bags, and some airlines restrict in-flight use.

faqs.q: What is the best power bank for a Windows laptop?
faqs.a: The best power bank for a Windows laptop is one that matches its USB-C charger wattage. Most Windows ultrabooks use 45 to 100 watts, so the Anker 25K 165W or Baseus Blade 100W works well, while the Anker 737 covers higher-watt models. Laptops with barrel-plug chargers cannot charge from a USB-C bank.

faqs.q: Can a power bank charge a MacBook with MagSafe?
faqs.a: Yes. MacBooks with MagSafe also charge through their USB-C or Thunderbolt ports, so any USB-C PD power bank with enough wattage works. A 14-inch MacBook Pro charges well at 100 watts, while a 16-inch model needs a 140-watt port, such as the Anker 737's, and a 240-watt cable for full speed.

bottomLine: Judge a laptop power bank on two numbers: the wattage of its best USB-C port and its capacity in watt-hours. Match the first to your laptop charger, expect the second to deliver about one full laptop charge, and pair the bank with a cable rated for the wattage you need. For most people that means the Anker 737. Step up to the Anker Prime 26K for two laptops, pick the Anker 25K 165W for cable-free travel, the UGREEN Nexode for value and the Baseus Blade for a slim ultrabook bank, and move to a station like the Anker SOLIX C300 DC when one charge is not enough. Skip unbranded banks with impossible capacity claims, and always keep your bank in your carry-on.
